problem: The caption says 'the Weibull starts lower and rises later'. For Weibull(2,1) the density near 0 behaves like 2t, while Gamma(2,1) behaves like t, so the Weibull is actually the highest of the three at small t (0.198 against 0.090 for gamma and 0.0002 for log-normal at t = 0.1). The Weibull also peaks earliest, at t = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, while gamma peaks at t = 1 and log-normal at about t = 0.779. The sentence reverses the shapes.
fix: 'The gamma curve is tallest at t = 2. Near t = 0 the Weibull is highest and rises fastest; it peaks first, at t ≈ 0.71, and then falls away quickly.'

problem: The y-axis maximum is 0.7, but the Weibull(2,1) density reaches about 0.858 at t ≈ 0.707 and Log-normal(0,0.5) reaches about 0.904 at t ≈ 0.779. Every sampled point above 0.7 has been dropped, so both plotted curves have gaps (Weibull jumps from x = 0.39 to x = 1.07, log-normal from x = 0.54 to x = 1.12) and their peaks are missing. The picture therefore shows the wrong shape for two of the three densities.
fix: Raise the y-axis maximum to about 1.0 and keep all sample points, so each curve is drawn continuously through its peak.

problem: The lead says all three distributions are defined on t > 0, but Sections 1 and 2 write t ≥ 0, and here 0 is genuinely in the support of the gamma and Weibull (the density is 0, finite or infinite at t = 0 depending on k or β). Only the log-normal excludes 0.
fix: Say in the lead that all three live on positive time, with gamma and Weibull allowed to start at t = 0 and log-normal defined only for t > 0.
